summary.text: The mixed layer is a layer of an ocean or lake in which active turbulence has stirred a range of depths until temperature and salinity are nearly uniform.
Because seawater holds far more heat than air, the top 2.5 m of the ocean stores as much heat as the entire atmosphere above it.
Its depth sets how much light marine life receives, so when it turns shallow in spring there is often a bloom of phytoplankton.

items.prompt: In the North Atlantic winter, the mixed layer deepens a great deal. What happens to the tiny drifting algae near the surface?

options.label: They thrive on the extra stirring
They get too little light, and chlorophyll drops
They sink and turn into ocean sediment
They are unaffected by how deep it gets

items.explain: In very deep mixed layers phytoplankton cannot get enough light, so winter deepening brings a strong fall in surface chlorophyll a.

items.prompt: Seawater stores far more heat than air does. The top 2.5 m of the ocean holds about as much heat as what?

options.label: The air in a large city
The lowest kilometre of air
A single summer thunderstorm
The whole atmosphere above it

items.explain: Because the specific heat of ocean water is much larger than that of air, the top 2.5 m holds as much heat as the entire atmosphere above.

items.prompt: On a cold night the surface water cools until it is denser than the water just below. What happens next?

options.label: It sinks, and convection stirs the layer
It stays on top as a cold, still lid
It rises higher and then evaporates
It spreads sideways without mixing

items.explain: When cooling raises surface density, convection occurs; this process forms the deepest mixed layers.

items.prompt: Breaking waves pump a great deal of energy into the top few meters of the sea. Why doesn't that energy stir the water very deep?

options.label: Salt in the water absorbs the energy
Waves only move water sideways
Most of it dissipates quite rapidly
Fish swimming below cancel it out

items.explain: Wave-driven turbulence injects a lot of energy into the upper few meters, but most of it dissipates relatively rapidly.

items.prompt: An oceanographer finds the bottom of the mixed layer by noting where temperature first differs from the surface by a set amount. Why does this work?

options.label: Temperature rises steadily all the way down
Light vanishes exactly at that depth
Currents come to a full stop at that depth
The layer is nearly uniform, then changes at its base

items.explain: The mixed layer is nearly uniform in temperature and salinity, and its bottom is marked by a gradient where water properties change.

items.prompt: Inside the mixed layer, temperature and salinity barely vary from top to bottom. What can still change sharply within it?

options.label: Salinity
Temperature
Current speed
Freezing point

items.explain: Although properties like temperature and salinity are nearly uniform, velocities may show significant shears within the mixed layer.

paragraphs.heading: A well-stirred top layer
paragraphs.text: The mixed layer is a layer of an ocean or lake where active turbulence has blended a range of depths together. Through the layer, properties such as temperature and salinity are nearly the same, although the speed of the water can still change sharply with depth. At the ocean surface, the turbulence comes from wind, from heat gained or lost at the surface, or from evaporation or sea ice formation that makes the water saltier.

paragraphs.heading: A huge store of heat
paragraphs.text: Seawater can hold far more heat than air. As a result, just the uppermost 2.5 m of ocean stores as much heat as the whole atmosphere above it. The heat needed to warm a mixed layer 2.5 m deep by 1 °C would be enough to warm the atmosphere by 1 °C. So the depth of this layer matters a great deal for how much temperatures swing in the open ocean and along coasts. The heat it stores also feeds global swings such as El Niño.

paragraphs.heading: Light, nutrients and blooms
paragraphs.text: How deep the mixed layer goes sets how much light, on average, reaches marine life. When it is very deep, phytoplankton, the tiny organisms of the sea, cannot get enough light to keep going. That is why surface chlorophyll a drops sharply in the North Atlantic winter, when the layer deepens. But deep mixing also restocks nutrients near the surface. So when the layer turns shallow in spring and light increases, phytoplankton often surge in what is called the spring bloom.

paragraphs.heading: What does the stirring
paragraphs.text: Three main energy sources stir the open-ocean mixed layer. Waves make turbulence near the surface, though most of that energy fades fast, and they can also drive Langmuir circulation, large eddies reaching tens of meters down. Wind-driven currents slide past one another at different speeds, and when that shear is strong enough it eats into the layered water below. Finally, when cooling, brine from freezing sea ice or evaporation makes the surface water heavier, convection sets in. This last process makes the deepest mixed layers, over 2000 m in places like the Labrador Sea.

paragraphs.heading: The bottom edge
paragraphs.text: At the base of the mixed layer, water properties start to change. Often there is a sudden temperature change, called a thermocline, and sometimes a sudden salinity change, called a halocline. Together they make a sudden change in density, called a pycnocline. Sharp changes in nutrients and oxygen, and a peak in chlorophyll, often sit at the base of the seasonal mixed layer too.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring its depth
paragraphs.text: Oceanographers usually find the depth of the mixed layer by measuring the water itself. Two common tests look for a set change in temperature or in density compared with the surface. A 1982 study by Levitus used a temperature change of 0.5 °C, while work by Kara and others in 2000 suggests a figure closer to .8 °C. Neither test means the water is actively mixing that deep at every moment. Instead, the depth shows how far mixing reaches over a few weeks.
